lessons.title: Quick check
lessons.objective: See what you already know about AI chatbots. There is no pass or fail.

items.heading: Before you start
items.body: Answer 5 quick questions. Just choose what you think. You will see how much you learned at the end of the module.

items.prompt: How does a chatbot usually create its answer?
options: It finds a finished answer on a website
It predicts likely words, one piece at a time
items.feedback: It predicts likely next pieces of text, one at a time.

items.prompt: When a chatbot reads your message, what does it work with?
options: Small pieces of text called tokens
The meaning, exactly like a person
items.feedback: Text is split into small pieces called tokens, which the model turns into numbers.

items.prompt: Which question will probably get the most useful answer?
options: I grow maize on a small, dry farm. Suggest 3 ways to save water, as a short list.
items.feedback: Giving context, a clear task and a format usually gets a more useful answer.

items.prompt: A chatbot answer sounds very confident. What does that tell you?
options: Nothing on its own: confident answers can still be wrong
It was checked by a teacher
items.feedback: Chatbots can state false information confidently. This is called a hallucination.

items.prompt: Which of these is safest to share with a chatbot?
options: A question about how volcanoes work
items.feedback: Keep personal details private. General questions are fine.

lessons.title: AI is a next-word guesser
lessons.objective: Explain in your own words how a chatbot builds an answer.

items.heading: What is inside a chatbot?
items.body: A chatbot like Gemini or ChatGPT runs on a large language model. The model was trained on a huge amount of text, such as books and websites. From all that text, it learned which words usually come after other words.

items.heading: It guesses, one piece at a time
items.body: When you ask a question, the model does not look up a finished answer. It guesses the most likely next word, adds it, and then guesses the next one. It repeats this again and again until the answer is complete. Let's try being the model.

items.prompt: I drink a cup of hot ___
items.feedback: The model picks words that often follow 'a cup of hot'. 'Shoe' or 'rain' almost never come next, so they get a tiny chance.

items.prompt: The sun rises in the ___
items.feedback: This phrase appears very often in text, so the model is very sure about the next word.

items.prompt: After school, I finish my ___
items.feedback: Several words could fit. The model chooses one of the likely ones. That is why the same question can get slightly different answers.

items.prompt: The farmer waters the ___
items.feedback: The model has seen 'farmer' and 'waters' near words like 'plants' and 'crops' many times.

items.prompt: Two plus two equals ___
items.feedback: The model gets this right because it has seen this sentence many times, not because it did the sum like a calculator. With rare or tricky questions, a likely-sounding word can be wrong.

items.heading: Key idea
items.body: A chatbot builds its answer one small piece at a time by choosing likely next words. Likely is not the same as true. That is why answers can sound perfect and still be wrong. You will see this in Lesson 4.

items.prompt: How does a chatbot usually write its answer?
options: It copies a finished answer from a website
It predicts likely next words, one piece at a time
A person types the answer very quickly
items.feedback: The model keeps predicting the next likely piece until the answer is complete.

items.prompt: Where did the model learn which words go together?
options: From a huge amount of text it was trained on
items.feedback: Training on lots of text taught the model common word patterns.

items.prompt: A chatbot's answer sounds confident and clear. Does that mean it is correct?
options: Yes, confident answers are always correct
No, the model chooses likely words, and likely is not always true
Only if the answer is long
items.feedback: Fluent text can still contain mistakes. Lesson 4 shows how to spot them.

lessons.title: Words become tokens
lessons.objective: Explain that a chatbot reads and writes text as small pieces called tokens.

items.heading: A chatbot does not read like you
items.body: When you type a message, the model first cuts your text into small pieces called tokens. A token can be a whole short word, part of a longer word, or a mark like a comma.

items.heading: Tokens become numbers
items.body: Each token is turned into a number. The model works with these numbers, not with letters or meanings like a person does. Then it predicts the next token, as you saw in Lesson 1.

items.prompt: Tap each sentence to see how it might be split into tokens.
items.feedback: Short, common words are often one token. Long or rare words are often split into parts. The exact split depends on the model.

items.prompt: Which word is more likely to be split into several tokens?
items.feedback: Long or less common words are often split into smaller parts.

items.prompt: What does the model do with each token?
options: Looks it up in a dictionary
items.feedback: Each token becomes a number, and the model works with those numbers.

items.heading: Why this matters
items.body: Because the model sees tokens and not single letters, it can make strange mistakes, like miscounting the letters in a word. It is very good at patterns in text, but it does not see words the way you do.

items.prompt: A chatbot says the word 'strawberry' has 2 letter r's. It has 3. What is one likely reason?
options: It sees tokens, not single letters
items.feedback: The model works with tokens, so counting single letters is surprisingly hard for it.

items.heading: Key idea
items.body: Your words become tokens, and tokens become numbers. The model predicts the next token again and again to build its answer.

lessons.title: Ask better, get better
lessons.objective: Write a clear prompt that gets a more useful answer.

items.heading: What is a prompt?
items.body: A prompt is what you type to the chatbot. The model uses your words as the start of its prediction. A vague prompt often gets a vague answer. A clear prompt usually gets a more useful one.

items.heading: Four parts of a clear prompt
items.body: 1. Role: who should the AI act as? 2. Context: what does it need to know about you? 3. Task: what exactly do you want? 4. Format: how should the answer look, for example a short list?

items.prompt: Make this weak prompt better. Add each part and watch the answer improve.
items.weak_answer: Crops are plants grown by people for food, fibre or other uses. There are many kinds of crops around the world, such as rice, wheat and maize.

parts.text: You are a friendly farming adviser.
I grow maize on a small farm where it rarely rains.
Answer as a short list, in simple words.

items.strong_answer:
1. Cover the soil around your plants with dry grass or leaves to keep it damp.
2. Water early in the morning or in the evening, when less water dries up.
3. Water the roots directly instead of spraying the whole field.
items.feedback: Same AI, much more useful answer. The clear prompt told it who you are, what you need and how to answer.

items.prompt: Which part is missing from this prompt: 'You are a science teacher. Explain photosynthesis.'?
items.feedback: It has a role and a task. Adding a format makes the answer easier to use.

items.heading: The creativity setting
items.body: Some AI tools have a setting called temperature. A low temperature makes answers more predictable. A higher temperature makes answers more varied and creative, but they can also drift off topic.

items.prompt: Move the slider to see how the same prompt can give different answers.
items.base_prompt: Write a one-line slogan for a school library.

settings.label: Medium
settings.answer: Every book is a door to a new world.

settings.label: High
settings.answer: Books are paper spaceships. Blast off at the library!

items.feedback: Higher temperature gives more surprising answers. For facts, predictable is better. For stories and slogans, a little creativity can help.

items.prompt: You need correct facts for a science test. Which temperature setting is best?
items.feedback: For facts, predictable answers are better. Creativity is useful for stories and ideas.

items.prompt: You wrote a very clear prompt. Does that make the answer always correct?
options: Yes, clear prompts always give true answers
No, clear prompts help, but the AI can still be wrong
Only if the prompt is long
items.feedback: A clear prompt usually gives a more useful answer, but it can still contain mistakes. Lesson 4 shows how to spot them.

items.heading: Key idea
items.body: Role, context, task and format make a clear prompt. Clear prompts get more useful answers, but you still need to check them.

lessons.title: When AI gets it wrong
lessons.objective: Spot a likely wrong AI answer and know how to check it.

items.heading: What is an AI hallucination?
items.body: Sometimes a chatbot states something false or made up, as if it were a fact. This is called a hallucination. The answer often sounds confident, so it is easy to believe.

items.heading: Why does it happen?
items.body: Remember Lesson 1: the model chooses likely words. It does not check each fact as it writes. Mistakes are more common with rare topics, but they can happen with any question, even a simple one. A chatbot can even invent names, numbers or studies that do not exist.

items.prompt: A chatbot gave these three sentences about honey. Which one did it make up?
options: People have eaten honey for thousands of years.
Bees make honey from the nectar of flowers.
Eating honey every day cures malaria.
items.feedback: There is no evidence that honey cures malaria. Always check health claims with a doctor, nurse or trusted health service.

items.prompt: Which sentence about capital cities is wrong?
options: Nairobi is the capital of Kenya.
Lima is the capital of Brazil.
Hanoi is the capital of Vietnam.
items.feedback: Lima is the capital of Peru. The capital of Brazil is Brasilia. A wrong fact can hide between two true ones.

items.prompt: You asked a chatbot to help with science homework about plants. Which part should you not trust without checking?
options: Plants use sunlight to make their own food.
Plants take in carbon dioxide from the air.
A 2019 study by Dr. Ana Lopes proved that plants grow 50% faster when people sing to them.
items.feedback: Chatbots can invent studies, names and numbers. Search for the study yourself before you use it. If you cannot find it, leave it out.

items.heading: How to check an AI answer
items.body: 1. Ask: where did this come from? 2. Check important facts in a second trusted source, such as a textbook, a teacher or an official website. 3. Take extra care with health, money and news. 4. If you cannot confirm it, do not share it.

items.prompt: What is an AI hallucination?
options: When the chatbot states false or made-up information as if it were true
When the chatbot answers very slowly
items.feedback: A hallucination is false or invented information presented as fact.

items.prompt: Can hallucinations happen with easy questions?
options: No, only with very hard questions
Yes, they are more common with rare topics but can happen with any question
No, never if the answer is short
items.feedback: Rare topics raise the risk, but any answer can contain a mistake.

items.prompt: A chatbot tells you a home remedy for a fever. What should you do?
options: Try it right away because the chatbot sounded sure
Share it with your family group first
Check with a doctor, nurse or trusted health source before using it
items.feedback: Health advice needs checking with a trusted human expert or official health source.

lessons.title: Use AI wisely
lessons.objective: Decide when to check an AI answer, protect your privacy, and use AI honestly.

items.heading: AI is a tool, you are in charge
items.body: AI can help you learn, write and explore ideas. But you decide what to trust, what to share and how to use it. Three habits help: check important facts, protect your privacy and be honest about AI help.

items.prompt: Sort each AI answer: is it low risk, or should you check it first?

cards.text: AI suggests five words that rhyme with 'light'.
AI says a new medicine cures diabetes.
AI gives you the deadline for your exam registration.
AI suggests a title for your poem.
AI says a scholarship will give you money if you send your bank details.
AI summarises a chapter you have already read, so you can compare it with the book.

items.feedback: Check anything about health, money, dates, news or offers that ask for personal details. Use official sources, a teacher or a trusted adult.

items.heading: Protect your privacy
items.body: What you type into a chatbot may be stored. Never share passwords, your home address, phone number, ID numbers or bank details. Ask general questions instead of sharing private ones.

items.prompt: Which of these should you never type into a chatbot?
items.feedback: Passwords and personal details must stay private.

items.heading: AI can be unfair too
items.body: AI learned from text written by people, and some of that text contains unfair ideas about groups of people. So AI answers can sometimes repeat those unfair ideas. If an answer treats a group unfairly, question it.

items.prompt: Why can AI answers sometimes be unfair to a group of people?
options: The AI learned from text that contains unfair ideas
The AI wants to be unkind
items.feedback: AI repeats patterns from its training text, including unfair ones.

items.heading: Be honest about AI help
items.body: Follow your school's rules about using AI. If you use AI to help with homework, say so. Use it to understand and practise, not to hand in work that is not yours.

items.prompt: Your teacher allows AI for brainstorming but not for writing essays. What should you do?
options: Use AI to write the whole essay
Use AI for ideas, then write the essay yourself
Copy an essay from a friend
items.feedback: Follow the rules and do your own writing. AI can help you think, not replace your work.

items.heading: Key idea
items.body: Check important facts. Keep personal details private. Watch for unfair answers. Be honest about AI help.

lessons.title: Final challenge
lessons.objective: Use everything from Module 1 in real-life situations.

items.prompt: Your cousin says the chatbot 'knows everything because it searches the internet each time'. What do you tell him?
options: Most chatbots predict likely words from patterns they learned; some apps add search, but not always
items.feedback: A chatbot builds answers by predicting likely next words. Some apps add a search tool, but that is a separate feature.

items.prompt: A chatbot keeps miscounting the letters in long words. What is the best explanation?
options: It reads text as tokens, not single letters
It is bad at English only
items.feedback: Words are split into tokens, so the model does not see each letter on its own.

items.prompt: You want help planning a 1-week revision timetable for 3 subjects. Which prompt is best?
options: You are a study coach. I have exams in maths, science and English in one week and 2 free hours each day. Make a daily plan as a table.
items.feedback: It gives a role, context, a clear task and a format.

items.prompt: Your friend's essay quotes a study the chatbot suggested, but you cannot find the study anywhere. What happened?
options: The chatbot may have invented it: a hallucination
items.feedback: Chatbots can invent studies, names and numbers. If you cannot find it, do not use it.

items.prompt: A message says 'AI confirms you won a prize. Send your phone number and bank details.' What do you do?
options: Do not share anything; check with a trusted adult or the official source
items.feedback: Never share personal or bank details. Offers that ask for them are often scams.

items.heading: Module complete: you are AI Smart!
items.body: You now know how chatbots build answers, why they use tokens, how to write clear prompts, how to spot mistakes, and how to use AI wisely. Compare your score with your Quick check to see how much you learned.
